notes.meaning: Job reflects on how fragile human life is for every person born into the world. Because human beings come from weak parents, their days on earth are few and filled with sorrow. Remembering that our days are short helps us turn to God for comfort.

Human life blooms quickly like a delicate flower, but it soon withers and is cut down by disease or age. A person is also like a fast-moving shadow that races across the ground and soon disappears. We should not put our final hope in earthly things that fade so quickly.

Job asks God why He watches such a weak and frail creature with such intense scrutiny. He wonders why the almighty Creator would bring a feeble mortal into a strict legal courtroom. Job pleads for God to look on him with mercy instead of harsh judgment.

Job acknowledges that every person is born with original sin, which means a sinful nature inherited from our parents. Since all human parents are flawed, no child can produce a pure life on their own. Only God's forgiving grace can make an unclean sinner clean.

differ.view: Job is teaching the doctrine of original sin, showing that every human inherits a corrupted nature from Adam.
The verse points to inherited human weakness and ceremonial defilement rather than the formal doctrine of original sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient Latin and Aramaic readings translate this verse as an affirmation that only God can make an unclean person clean.

notes.meaning: God has already decided the exact length of every human life before it begins. No person can live a single month or day beyond the boundary God has set. We can rest in knowing that our lives are in God's sovereign hands.

Job asks God to turn His searching gaze away so that he can find a moment of relief from pain. Like a hired worker who looks forward to resting when his hard day of labor is finished, Job longs for ease before he dies. He simply asks for a brief breathing space before life ends.

Job points out that even a tree has a kind of hope when an axe cuts it down. Fresh green sprouts can push out from the old stump and keep growing. Nature shows how plant life can revive after being brought low.

A tree's root system may grow old in the dirt, and its main stump may seem dead and dry. Even though all outward signs of life have vanished, the root is not entirely lost. Hidden vitality remains quietly beneath the soil.

As soon as the dry root senses the presence of water, it buds and produces fresh branches like a young plant. The moisture revives the stump the way fresh air revives someone who has fainted. Job uses this picture to highlight the sharp contrast between resilient trees and dying humans.

Unlike a tree that can sprout again, a human being who dies does not return to life in this present world. Even the strongest and most powerful person loses all physical strength and breathes his last. When death arrives, a person's earthly place knows him no more.

Job compares human death to water that drains away from an inland lake or a river that completely dries up in a drought. Once the water is gone, the riverbed lies empty and parched. In the same way, mortal life drains away and leaves an empty place on earth.

When people die, they lie down in the grave as if sleeping in a bed and do not rise to their old lives. They will not wake up to resume everyday earthly tasks while this present world lasts. Traditional readers see this as pointing to the sleep of death until the final resurrection.

differ.view: Job was speaking from extreme grief and limited knowledge of the afterlife, describing death as final without intending to teach settled doctrine.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The phrase about the heavens passing away describes the permanence of death rather than the end of the universe or a bodily resurrection.

notes.meaning: Job prays that God would hide him in Sheol, the place of the dead, like a treasure tucked safely away from a storm. He asks God to set a time when His anger will pass and He will remember Job with favor. This plea shows a faint hope that death will not be the final word.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Latin translations used the word hell for Sheol here, understanding it as the resting place of departed souls before Christ.

notes.meaning: Job asks whether a man can live again after dying, knowing a person cannot return to this earthly life. He resolves to wait through his hard time of suffering until his final renewal comes. Christians have long read this as waiting with hope for the resurrection.

differ.view: Job's question is an expression of hope that God will raise him to life in the world to come after his earthly struggle ends.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Job's question expects the answer no, expressing deep despair about any possible life after physical death.

notes.meaning: Job expresses confidence that God will call out to him one day and that he will gladly answer. The Creator genuinely cares for the people He has made and will not abandon them to the dust forever. We can be encouraged that God deeply values each person He created.

In his present pain, Job feels as though God is tracking his steps only to catch him in sin. Yet he looks ahead to a time when God will protect his steps instead of keeping a record of his wrongs. God's ultimate desire for His children is mercy rather than constant fault-finding.

Job worries that God is tying up his sins in a sealed bag to preserve them for judgment. Yet sealing away and covering over sins can also mean that God hides our guilt so it is pardoned completely. When God forgives our wrongdoing, He covers it so it can never condemn us.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Job is asking for legal acquittal, picturing his sins sealed in a pouch so they are hidden and forgiven forever.

notes.meaning: Job slides back into sadness by comparing human frailty to great mountains that crumble into dust. Even massive rocks get pushed out of place by earthquakes and storms. If even the strongest parts of creation collapse, weak humans cannot hope to stand forever on their own.

Gentle water wears away hard stones over time, and raging flash floods wash away the soil. In a similar way, constant suffering wears away human strength and destroys earthly hopes. Difficult trials can make a person feel as though their life is being eroded to nothing.

God's power always overcomes human resistance, and every mortal eventually passes away into death. When death comes, God changes the person's pale face and sends them away from earthly life. Human beings must realize how small they are before the mighty power of God.

Once a person dies, he knows nothing about what happens to his family on earth. If his children gain honor or fall into poverty, the dead parent is completely unaware of it. Death cuts off all connection with the joys and sorrows of this present world.

In severe sickness and death, a person's attention is entirely taken up by his own bodily pain and inward grief. The dying person cannot focus on others because his own suffering fills his whole mind. Job honestly describes how lonely and heavy physical torment can feel.
